questions.knowledge_point: Integrating the Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=-4x,$ then, 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-4\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}5{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{-4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{u}(-\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})}{e}^{u}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({e}^{u}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({3}^{-4}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\frac{1}{{3}^{4}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\frac{1}{81}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(-\frac{80}{81}) \\  & =\frac{100}{81}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating the Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=4x+1,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $9$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}4{e}^{4x+1}\,\text{d}x & =4{\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{4x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4{\int }_{1}^{9}{e}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{9}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}\,{|}_{1}^{9} \\  & ={e}^{9}-{e}^{1} \\  & ={e}^{9}-e\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating the Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\frac{x}{2}-1,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,2\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{x/2\,-\,1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,{e}^{u}+C \\  & =2\,{e}^{x/2\,-\,1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating the Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
First, we notice that

$$
\int {e}^{z}{e}^{z}\,\text{d}z=\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z.
$$

If we let $u=2z$, then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}z=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}z & =\int {e}^{2z}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2z}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {e}^{u}+C \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2z}}{2}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a General Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=x-1,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-1$ | $1$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{5}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{5}^{u}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{{5}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\,{|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}({5}^{1}-{5}^{-1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}(5-\frac{1}{5}) \\  & =\frac{24}{5\operatorname{ln}⁡5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a General Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=\frac{x}{3},$ then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\text{d}u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {6}^{x/3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {6}^{u}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {6}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\frac{{6}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {6}^{x/3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=6x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $6$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of  $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{3}^{6x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{3}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}{3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}){|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(729-1) \\  & =\frac{728}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{364}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a General Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
If we let $u=1-x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1\,⟹\,-\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $0$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}2\cdot {4}^{1-x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{0}2\cdot {4}^{u}(-1)\text{d}u \\  & =-2{\int }_{1}^{0}{4}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2(\frac{{4}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}){|}_{1}^{0} \\  & =-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}({4}^{0}-{4}^{1}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}(1-4) \\  & =\frac{6}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating the Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we let $u=1-3x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = -3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = -\dfrac 1 3 \textrm d u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{1-3x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{1-3x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a General Exponential Function With a Linear Exponent
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If we let $u=5+4x,$ then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} = 4\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d x = \dfrac 1 4 \textrm d u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {3}^{5+4x}\,\text{d}x & =\int {3}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int {3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{3}^{5+4x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$
